name: Cyril and Methodius
otherNames: Constantine the Philosopher, Cyril's name until he took the monk's name Cyril in Rome, weeks before he died, by the Life of Constantine and the Italian Legend
knownFor: Two brothers of Thessalonica, sent from Constantinople in the 860s to Moravia, whose ruler had asked for teachers in his people's own language. Constantine made letters for the Slavs, and the brothers turned the church's services into Slavic. Against clergy who said God may be praised only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, they held that every people may praise God in its own tongue; in 880 Pope John VIII allowed the Mass to be sung in Slavonic, with the Gospel read first in Latin. Their disciples carried the letters and the Slavic services to Bulgaria.
dates: Ninth century. No source used here gives either brother's year of birth. Count Lützow dates the Moravian embassy to Constantinople to 862, the world census to 863; Johann Ginzel reckons their arrival in Moravia to 863. Constantine died in Rome on 14 February, aged 42, in the year 6377 from the creation, by the Life of Constantine; S. H. Cross gives 869, and Ginzel 868. Methodius died on 6 April, by the Life of Methodius, whose year is garbled in the held copy; Lützow and Ginzel give 885
place: Thessalonica, their home, a Greek city where Slavic was spoken too; Constantinople, where Constantine studied and taught; Moravia, their mission, in what is now the Czech Republic; Pannonia, the see Methodius was made bishop for; Venice, where Constantine answered the Latin clergy; Rome, where Cyril died and was buried in the church of St Clement; Cherson, where the Italian Legend says Constantine found the relics of Clement of Rome
role: Brothers and missionaries: Constantine (Cyril), scholar, teacher of philosophy and maker of the Slavic letters, a monk only at the end; Methodius, governor of a Slavic district, then monk, then bishop and archbishop for the Slavs

keyWorks.title: The Slavic letters
keyWorks.about: which Pope John VIII calls the Slavonic letters found by Constantine the Philosopher, and the Lives say God revealed to him after prayer. S. H. Cross, and the census with him, says Constantine made the Glagolitic letters, not the Cyrillic; Count Lützow says his alphabet became known as Cyrillic. No held text describes the letters' shapes

keyWorks.title: Slavonic translations
keyWorks.about: the Gospel, the Apostle, the Psalter and chosen services, by the two brothers, as the Life of Methodius says; it adds that Methodius later put the rest of the Scriptures, except Maccabees, into Slavonic in six months. Cross says this six-month tradition is generally regarded as apocryphal. None of the brothers' own Slavonic is held

traces: After Methodius died, Wiching, whom he had condemned, took the see, and the disciples were driven out. Clement, Naum and Angelarius crossed the Danube to Bulgaria, where, the Life of Clement says, Prince Boris thanked God for them.
The Life of Clement says Clement became "the first bishop of the Bulgarian tongue" and wrote plain sermons for every feast, because Bulgarian priests could barely follow Greek.
The Russian Primary Chronicle, compiled in Kiev by 1116, says the writing first made for the Moravians and their neighbouring Slavs exists also in Rus and among the Danube Bulgarians.

The Life of Clement names Gorazd, Clement, Naum, Angelarius and Sava as the brothers' chief disciples; the Life of Methodius says he named Gorazd, a man of the Moravians' own country, learned in Latin books, to follow him.
remembered: In S. H. Cross's English of the Russian Primary Chronicle, "The Slavs rejoiced to hear the greatness of God extolled in their native tongue."
The Life of Constantine says that in Rome a painted image was set over his tomb, with lamps kept burning day and night.
Ginzel reports that in 1380 Bishop John of Olomouc ordered their feast kept on 9 March, calling them the diocese's fathers, apostles and chief patrons.

Augustin Theiner dedicated his Vatican documents of 1863 to Joseph George Strossmayer, bishop of Bosnia or Diakovo, and wrote that the work kept the thousandth-year feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, which the Church celebrated that year.

uncertain: How close the Lives are. Most of what is known comes from the Life of Constantine and the Life of Methodius, written in Slavonic by the brothers' followers and judged by their editors to be close to the events. They survive only in copies made centuries later, from the 14th and 15th centuries on, and are read here in 19th-century Latin translations. Wilhelm Wattenbach rated their historical worth very highly. Ginzel, who writes against the Greek schism, holds the Life of Methodius to be a Greek schismatic's work made to look contemporary.
The Italian Legend. The Bollandists think it very probably the work of Gauderich of Velletri, a bishop of the brothers' time, and Ginzel trusts it.
That God revealed the letters is the Lives' own claim. That Constantine made a Slavic alphabet is widely accepted; which alphabet is contested, so the brief says "Slavic letters".

Which pope. The Life of Methodius says Pope Nicholas received them and ordained Methodius priest; the Life of Constantine names Hadrian; the Italian Legend says Nicholas had died and Hadrian received them.

Were both made bishops? The Italian Legend says Hadrian made both brothers bishops. The two Lives say Constantine took the monk's habit and died, and Methodius was made priest, then bishop for the Slavs of Pannonia.

How long they stayed in Moravia. The Life of Methodius says three years, the Life of Constantine forty months, the Italian Legend four and a half years. Ginzel follows the Legend and calls the Life wrong.
The year Constantine died. Cross gives 869; Ginzel 868.
The day Methodius died. The Life of Methodius gives 6 April, in the year Ginzel works out as 885. Ginzel reports that Wattenbach thought a death on so high a feast suspicious, and defends the date.

His prison. The Life of Methodius says the enemy of the Moravian ruler and his bishops sent him to Swabia and held him two and a half years, until the pope barred them from saying Mass. Count Lützow says the German governors seized him and handed him as a prisoner to the German bishops.

The Salzburg account is hostile, written by his opponents in his lifetime. It says he "partly" cheapened the Latin Masses in the people's eyes. Ginzel and Bartholomäus Kopitar date it to 873; Ginzel reports that Joseph Assemani and Wilhelm Wattenbach give 871.

Rome's ruling was not settled at once. In 879 Pope John VIII repeated an earlier ban on singing Mass in Slavonic, while letting Methodius preach in it, before allowing it in 880. A later letter under Stephen V's name speaks against Methodius; Ginzel prints it as spurious.

The Life of Clement carries Archbishop Theophylact's name (about 1100); Miklosich held it the work of a Bulgarian who had lived with Clement, in the early tenth century. Either way it is a generation or more later.
The six-month Bible. Cross says it is generally regarded as apocryphal. The Chronicle's report that Constantine went to Bulgaria has, by Cross, no basis.

The renderings are from Latin translations of the Slavonic Lives (Dümmler and Miklosich for the Life of Constantine, Miklosich for the Life of Methodius), since no readable Slavonic is held; the pope's words and the Salzburg complaint are rendered from their Latin originals.

briefReferences: Life of Constantine, lines 20217–20233: Moravia asks for a teacher in its own language; the emperor sends the tired philosopher; "if they have letters for their language"; "who can write words on water"; the letters made after prayer.
Life of Methodius, lines 12201–12219: Rastislav's embassy; "you are Thessalonians, and all Thessalonians speak pure Slavonic"; the letters made.
Life of Constantine, lines 20256–20268: the services turned into Slavic; the Latin clergy who said God chose only three languages.
Life of Constantine, lines 20292–20314: Venice, the Latin bishops, priests and monks, and his answer.
Life of Constantine, lines 20379–20445: Rome, the pope comes out to meet them with Clement's relics; the monk's name Cyril; his death on 14 February, aged 42.
Life of Methodius, lines 12249–12365: his last words to Methodius; Methodius bishop for Pannonia; held two and a half years in Swabia.
Salzburg Conversio: the "Greek" with "newly invented Slavic letters" who partly cheapened the Latin Masses.
Pope John VIII, letter of 880 to Svatopluk: the Slavonic letters found by Constantine, Slavonic Mass allowed, the Gospel read first in Latin, and the three chief languages.
Life of Methodius, lines 12540–12551; his death on 6 April; Lützow for 885. Life of Clement (Latin extract in Ginzel): Wiching set up, the disciples driven out.
Life of Clement, PG 126: Clement, Naum and Angelarius to Bulgaria; Boris thanks God; Clement "the first bishop of the Bulgarian tongue"; the plain sermons.
Russian Primary Chronicle, tr. Cross: the writing first made for the Moravians, found in Rus and among the Danube Bulgarians; Cross's introduction for 869 and the dating.
Dümmler's introduction to the Life of Constantine and Ginzel on the Life of Methodius: the Lives written by followers, kept in late copies.
World census, Cyrillo-Methodian Slavic Christianity: their tradition, and the Czech Republic for Moravia.
